prompt: Which slide better supports a speech about how much water household activities use?

options.feedback: The audience will read the paragraph instead of listening, and the speaker is tempted to read it aloud. The textbook's advice: one message per slide.
One graph, one point, and a title that states the takeaway. The speaker explains; the slide shows.

prompt: What is the biggest problem with this slide?

options.text: Competing elements break unity, so the audience doesn't know where to look
options.feedback: Yes. Section 9.4 lists unity and emphasis among the design principles. "Just because you can doesn't mean you should."
The title is not the main issue.

prompt: What would most improve this slide?

options.feedback: The textbook strongly discourages sound effects on slides.

options.text: Increase contrast between text and background, and enlarge the text
options.feedback: Yes. If the back row cannot read it, the slide fails at its job. Strong contrast also supports viewers with low vision.

options.text: Switch to a decorative script font
options.feedback: Decorative fonts are usually harder to read from a distance.

prompt: Which slide makes its point faster?

options.feedback: Extra effects and a vague title make the audience work to find the point.
A plain bar graph with a title that states the takeaway is processed almost instantly.

prompt: You have four short points on a slide. How should they appear?

options.text: All at once, so the audience can read ahead
options.feedback: Audiences read ahead and stop listening. Control what they see.

options.text: One at a time as you discuss each point
options.feedback: Yes. The textbook notes that controlled entrance animation keeps attention on you and the current point.

options.text: Each spinning in with a different effect
options.feedback: Mixed, flashy effects break consistency and distract.
